title: Remote Work & Team Collaboration: Leading Distributed Teams
subtitle: Run a distributed team that writes things down, keeps its promises and makes decisions without endless calls.
description: An advanced, practical course for women who lead, coordinate or advise teams spread across cities and countries. You will set up async-first working agreements, a shared workspace, status updates, decision records and meetings that produce results, then audit a real team, scope an improvement project and build your own accountability system and evidence portfolio.
outcomes: Write complete asynchronous messages, briefs and weekly status updates that colleagues can act on without a meeting
Draft a team working agreement with channels, response times and overlap hours calculated across time zones
Set up a single source of truth for files, tasks and decisions, with safe sharing and low-bandwidth options
Run remote meetings with agendas, roles, written summaries and a decision log, using DACI for decisions
Audit a distributed team, prioritise fixes and price a scoped improvement project with change control
Keep a personal accountability system and present a three-piece remote collaboration portfolio
audience: Women who coordinate, lead or support teams, volunteer networks or clients across locations and want to do it professionally, including those preparing for remote team lead or operations roles.
tools: A smartphone or laptop with internet access
A free Google account (Drive, Docs, Sheets, Calendar) or Microsoft 365
A messaging app your team uses, such as WhatsApp, Slack or Microsoft Teams
A free task board such as Trello or a shared Google Sheet
A notebook or task app for your personal commitment list

modules.title: How Distributed Teams Really Work
modules.overview: Distributed teams succeed when they replace office habits with deliberate ones: writing first, agreeing how and when to communicate, and building trust through visible work. This module gives you the operating model, a working agreement you can adopt with any team, and the leadership habits that keep people connected across distance.

lessons.title: Async-first: the operating model of distributed teams
objectives: Explain the difference between synchronous and asynchronous work and the cost of each
Choose the right channel for a message using a simple escalation ladder
Rewrite a vague chat request into a complete asynchronous message
Describe the kinds of distributed teams you are likely to join or lead

blocks.text: A distributed team is any team whose members do not share one workplace every day. It might be a company with staff in Lagos, Nairobi and London, a Nigerian NGO with coordinators in every state, a volunteer network spread across several African countries, or a freelancer working with a client abroad. What they all lose is the office: the quick question across the desk, the overheard update, the manager who can see who is busy. What they must build instead is a way of working that does not depend on everyone being online at the same moment.

blocks.name: remote-team
blocks.alt: Team members working from different locations connected online
blocks.caption: A distributed team shares goals and documents, not a room.

blocks.text: Two modes of communication

**Synchronous** (sync) communication happens in real time: a phone call, a video meeting, a live chat where both people reply at once. **Asynchronous** (async) communication does not need an instant reply: a shared document, an email, a task comment, a well-written WhatsApp or Slack message that the reader can answer within agreed hours. Neither is better in every case. Sync is fast for feelings, conflict, brainstorming and emergencies. Async is better for updates, decisions that need thought, and anything that people in other time zones must read.

Many mature remote companies describe themselves as **async-first** (sometimes called async by default). GitLab, which publishes its whole remote handbook online, is a well known example. Async-first does not mean no meetings. It means a meeting is a deliberate choice, and the default is to write things down where everyone can find them. The benefit is that people can do focused work for long stretches, and a colleague eight hours away is not left out of decisions.

head: Situation
Better mode
Why
rows: Async (written update in the team channel or document)
Everyone reads it in their own working hours and it stays on record
Async proposal first, short call only if comments stall
People need time to read the options and numbers
Tone is easily misread in text
Website down during a campaign launch
Minutes matter; nobody should wait for a reply
Ideas build quickly live; the record must be written

blocks.text: The escalation ladder
A simple rule keeps a team calm: start with the least interrupting channel that will still work in time, and move up only when you must. Each step up interrupts more people and costs more attention.

blocks.title: The escalation ladder
items: Phone call: emergencies only
Video call: conflict, complex talks
Direct message: needed today
Team channel: needed this week
Shared document or task comment
blocks.caption: Begin at the wide base and climb only when urgency or emotion demands it.

blocks.text: Writing a message that does not need a meeting

The core skill of async work is writing a message complete enough that the reader can act without asking you anything. A useful check is the **five parts**: context (what this is about), the ask (exactly what you need), the deadline (when, with the time zone), the options or your recommendation, and where the supporting material lives. Put the ask in the first line, because many people read only the preview on their phone.

blocks.title: Worked example: turning a vague ping into a complete async message
blocks.context: For example, Amaka coordinates a training programme. Her colleague Tunde in Abuja and the funder's officer in London must approve a venue. Her first draft in the team chat was: "Hi, are you free? Need to talk about the venue."
steps: She notices the draft has no ask, no deadline and forces a live conversation.
First line: "Decision needed by Thursday 5 pm Lagos time (WAT): approve Venue B for the March workshop."
Context: two venues were quoted; Venue A is about 450,000 naira for two days, Venue B about 380,000 naira (approximate quotes, valid for 7 days).
Recommendation: Venue B, because it has a backup generator and is 10 minutes from the bus park; the difference is 70,000 naira (450,000 minus 380,000).
Where to look: both quotes and photos are in the shared folder "March Workshop / Venues", with the link pasted.
Fallback: "If I hear nothing by the deadline I will book Venue B so we keep the date."
blocks.result: Tunde approves with a thumbs-up and one comment; the funder replies the next morning in her own working hours. No meeting was needed and the decision is on record.

blocks.title: Silence is not agreement unless you say so
blocks.text: A stated fallback ("if no objection by Thursday, I will proceed") turns silence into a clear rule. Use it only for decisions you are allowed to make, and always say what you will do.
Where these skills are used

items: **Fully remote companies** where everyone works from home or co-working spaces and there is no head office.
**Hybrid teams** where some people share an office and others dial in; the remote people are easily forgotten unless the team writes things down.
**Multi-site organisations** such as NGOs, banks or churches with offices in several cities or countries.
**Contractor and freelance networks** where a client brings together people from different firms and countries for a project.
**Volunteer networks** where people give a few hours a week, often by phone, and cannot attend long calls.

blocks.text: In every one of these, people who lead, coordinate or support the team are judged less on how many hours they are online and more on whether others can see progress, find decisions and rely on what was promised. That is what the rest of this course builds.

takeaways: Sync is for emotion, emergencies and fast idea building; async is for updates, considered decisions and anything across time zones.
Async-first means meetings are a deliberate choice and the record is written.
Climb the escalation ladder only as far as urgency or emotion requires.
A complete async message has context, ask, deadline with time zone, recommendation and a link to the material.

activity.title: Rewrite three messages
steps: Find three recent work or community messages you sent that started with "Hi" or "Are you free?".
For each, decide which rung of the escalation ladder it really needed.
Rewrite each one using the five parts, with the ask in the first line and a deadline that includes the time zone.
Add a fallback line to any message where silence should allow you to proceed.
activity.evidence: A note or document showing each original message beside its rewrite and the ladder level you chose.

lessons.title: The team working agreement: channels, response times and overlap hours
objectives: List the sections of a team working agreement
Calculate shared overlap hours for a team across several time zones
Set response-time expectations for each channel
Draft a one-page working agreement for a real or practice team

blocks.text: Most remote frustration comes from unspoken expectations. One person thinks a WhatsApp message deserves a reply within ten minutes; another checks messages twice a day. One person keeps files on their laptop; another expects them in the shared drive. A **team working agreement** (also called a team charter or communication charter) writes these expectations down so they can be discussed, agreed and changed. It is short, usually one or two pages, and every new member reads it in their first week.

blocks.name: agreement
blocks.alt: Two people shaking hands over a written agreement
blocks.caption: A working agreement turns guesses about each other into shared rules.

blocks.text: What goes in the agreement

head: Section
What it answers
Example entry
rows: Task board for work items; team channel for updates; WhatsApp only for urgent or field issues
How fast replies are expected, per channel
Task comments: within 1 working day; direct messages: same working day; phone: emergencies, answer at once
When each person works and when the team is reachable together
Core overlap 2 pm to 4 pm WAT, Monday to Thursday
The single source of truth for files and decisions
Shared drive folders by project; decisions logged in the Decision Log document
Which meetings exist and their rules
One 45-minute weekly call with agenda posted 24 hours before
How people show they are away or focused
Status set to "Focus" or "Away"; leave dates on the shared calendar

blocks.text: Working out overlap hours

Overlap hours are the times when everyone is inside their normal working day. To find them, convert every person's hours into one reference time, usually **UTC** (Coordinated Universal Time), then find where the ranges meet. Nigeria uses West Africa Time (WAT), which is UTC+1 all year with no daylight saving. Kenya uses East Africa Time, UTC+3, also with no daylight saving. The United Kingdom is UTC+0 in winter and UTC+1 in summer (British Summer Time), and Toronto is UTC-5 in winter and UTC-4 in summer. Because some countries change their clocks, **overlap can shift twice a year**, so check it in March and in October or November.

blocks.title: Worked example: a four-city team in January
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma leads a project team in January. Members work 9 am to 5 pm local time in Lagos (UTC+1), Nairobi (UTC+3), London (UTC+0) and Toronto (UTC-5).
steps: Lagos 9 to 17 local is 08:00 to 16:00 UTC (subtract 1 hour).
Nairobi 9 to 17 local is 06:00 to 14:00 UTC (subtract 3 hours).
London 9 to 17 local is 09:00 to 17:00 UTC (no change in winter).
Toronto 9 to 17 local is 14:00 to 22:00 UTC (add 5 hours).
All four together: the latest start is 14:00 UTC (Toronto) and the earliest finish is 14:00 UTC (Nairobi), so there is no shared hour at all.
Without Toronto: 09:00 to 14:00 UTC, which is 10 am to 3 pm in Lagos, 5 hours of overlap.
Toronto with Lagos and London: 14:00 to 16:00 UTC, which is 3 pm to 5 pm in Lagos and 9 am to 11 am in Toronto.
blocks.result: Ifeoma does not force a four-city meeting. She sets a weekly 3 pm WAT call for Lagos, London and Toronto, a 10 am WAT check-in that includes Nairobi, and makes the written weekly update the place where all four meet.

blocks.title: One UTC day for Ifeoma's team
items: 06:00 Nairobi starts
08:00 Lagos starts
09:00 London starts
14:00 Nairobi ends, Toronto starts
16:00 Lagos ends
17:00 London ends
blocks.caption: Converting everyone to UTC shows at a glance where overlap exists and where it disappears.

blocks.title: Use a time zone tool, then check by hand
blocks.text: World clock apps on Android and iPhone, Google Calendar's secondary time zone setting and free web planners can show several cities at once. Still do the arithmetic once yourself, because a wrong city choice in a tool is easy to miss.
Response times that people can keep

Response-time rules must be realistic for the slowest normal situation, not the best day. A coordinator in a rural area with unstable power and costly data cannot promise a ten-minute reply. A good agreement separates channels by urgency and gives one clear route for emergencies, so that nobody feels they must watch every chat all evening. It also protects rest: if the agreement says messages after 6 pm local time can wait until the next working day, people can switch off their notifications without guilt.

items: List every channel the team actually uses today, including personal WhatsApp.
Give each channel one main purpose and remove duplicates.
Agree a reply window for each channel, written in working hours or days, not "ASAP".
Name the single emergency route and what counts as an emergency.
Collect everyone's working hours, convert to UTC and mark the overlap.
Share the draft, invite comments for a week, then publish the agreed version with a review date.

blocks.title: Agree it together
blocks.text: A charter written by the leader alone and announced is often ignored. Draft it, ask for comments in writing, and change it. People keep rules they helped shape.

takeaways: A one-page working agreement replaces unspoken expectations with shared rules.
Convert all hours to UTC to find overlap, and recheck when clocks change in Europe and North America.
Nigeria (WAT, UTC+1) and Kenya (EAT, UTC+3) do not use daylight saving.
Set reply windows per channel and one clear emergency route.

activity.title: Draft your team's working agreement
steps: Choose a real team, volunteer group or practice team of at least three people.
Write each person's working hours and convert them to UTC; mark the overlap.
Fill in the seven sections from the table above in one page.
Share the draft with at least two team members and record their comments.
Publish a revised version with a review date.
activity.evidence: The one-page agreement, your UTC overlap calculation and a screenshot or note of the comments you received.

lessons.title: Trust at a distance: visibility, accountability and psychological safety
objectives: Explain why remote trust rests on visible, reliable work rather than presence
Run a useful one-to-one meeting with a remote team member
Handle disagreement in text before it becomes conflict
Apply practices that make quieter and low-bandwidth members heard

blocks.text: In an office, a manager often judges commitment by who arrives early and who looks busy. Remote teams cannot do that, and they should not try. Trust on a distributed team is built on three visible things: **people do what they said, by when they said, and say early when they cannot**. Leaders who try to replace presence with surveillance, such as demanding cameras on all day or counting online minutes, usually damage trust and get worse work.

blocks.name: team-spirit
blocks.caption: Trust grows when people can see progress and feel safe to speak.

blocks.text: Manage outcomes, not hours

Agree what a good result looks like, the deadline and who owns it, then let people organise their own time. This matters especially where members juggle family duties, power cuts and commuting to a place with stable internet. A useful habit is the **commitment message**: when you accept a task, you reply with what you will deliver and by when. When something slips, you post an update before the deadline, not after it.

blocks.title: The remote trust cycle
items: Make a clear commitment
Deliver or flag early
Work is visible to others
Others rely on you more
blocks.caption: Each kept or honestly renegotiated promise makes the next one easier to believe.

blocks.text: Psychological safety

Psychological safety, a term developed by Harvard Business School professor Amy Edmondson, means people believe they will not be punished or humiliated for speaking up with ideas, questions, concerns or mistakes. Remote teams need it more, not less, because problems hidden at a distance grow quietly. You build it by thanking people who raise bad news early, by admitting your own mistakes in the team channel, and by asking direct questions such as "What could go wrong with this plan?" rather than "Any questions?".
The remote one-to-one

A regular one-to-one (1:1) is the leader's most important meeting. Keep a shared running document for each person, so both of you add topics during the week and nothing is lost. A practical rhythm is 30 minutes every one or two weeks, by voice call if data is costly.

items: **Their agenda first:** what is on your mind, what is blocking you?
**Progress against commitments**, using the task board rather than memory.
**Feedback both ways:** one thing to keep doing, one thing to change, and ask what you as leader should change.
**Growth:** a skill they want to build this quarter.
**Actions written in the shared document** before you hang up.

blocks.text: Disagreement in text

Written messages lose tone, and short replies can read as cold. Two rules prevent most remote conflict. First, **assume good intent and ask before reacting**: "When you wrote 'this won't work', do you mean the timeline or the budget?" Second, **move to voice after two rounds**: if a disagreement has gone back and forth twice in a chat, call, settle it, then post a written summary so others see the outcome.

blocks.title: Worked example: a tense thread
blocks.context: For example, Zainab, a programme officer in Kano, posts a draft report. Femi, the finance lead in Lagos, replies in the team channel: "These numbers are wrong again." Zainab feels embarrassed in front of twelve people.
steps: Chiamaka, the team lead, sees the thread and messages Femi directly: "Can you list the specific lines so Zainab can fix them?"
Femi lists two lines: transport was entered as 85,000 naira but receipts total 58,000 naira, a transposed figure; and one per diem was counted twice.
Chiamaka calls Zainab for five minutes, shares the two lines, and asks what would help; Zainab suggests a shared checklist before reports are posted.
Zainab corrects the report. The transport line drops by 27,000 naira (85,000 minus 58,000).
Chiamaka posts in the channel: "Report corrected, thanks Zainab and Femi. From next month we will use a two-line finance check before posting drafts."
In the next working agreement review, the team adds: "Give critical feedback with specific lines, in a comment on the document rather than in the main channel."
blocks.result: The error is fixed, Zainab is not shamed, and the team gains a process that prevents the same problem.

blocks.text: Including everyone

items: Rotate meeting times when overlap is unfair, so the same people do not always join at night.
Send agendas early and accept written input from people who cannot join.
In calls, invite quieter people by name and use the chat for written contributions.
Offer audio-only or voice-note options for members on limited data.
Create small informal spaces, such as a weekly 15-minute optional chat or a channel for wins and photos, because remote teams lose casual connection.

blocks.title: Monitoring tools and privacy
blocks.text: Screenshot or keystroke tracking software collects personal data. In Nigeria, the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 governs how personal data is collected and used. Do not install monitoring on anyone's device without a lawful basis, clear written notice and advice from your organisation's data protection lead.

takeaways: Remote trust comes from clear commitments, early flags and visible work, not from hours online.
Psychological safety means people can raise problems without fear; reward early bad news.
Keep a shared running document for every one-to-one.
Ask before reacting in text, and move to voice after two rounds of disagreement.

activity.title: Set up a one-to-one document
steps: Create a shared document titled with your name and a colleague's name (or a practice partner).
Add the five headings from the one-to-one list above.
Hold a 20 to 30 minute call using the document, and write actions before ending.
Afterwards, write two sentences on what felt different from an unstructured chat.
activity.evidence: The one-to-one document with actions recorded and your two-sentence reflection.

quiz.q: A colleague in Nairobi needs your input on choosing between two printers, with prices attached, by Friday. What is the best first channel?
options: A written async message or document comment with the options, your recommendation and a deadline
A phone call after work hours
Wait until the next weekly meeting
quiz.explain: The decision needs thought and spans time zones, so a complete async message is best. Climb the ladder only if comments stall.

quiz.q: Which first line best follows async-first writing?
options: Are you free for a quick call?
Approval needed by Tuesday 12 noon WAT: sign off the training budget of 1.2 million naira
quiz.explain: The ask and deadline with time zone come first, so the reader knows what to do even from a phone preview.

quiz.q: Lagos staff work 9 am to 5 pm WAT and London staff work 9 am to 5 pm UK time. In January, what is the overlap in Lagos time?
quiz.explain: In winter London is UTC+0 and Lagos UTC+1. London 9 am is 10 am in Lagos, and Lagos finishes at 5 pm, so overlap is 10 am to 5 pm WAT.

quiz.q: Why should a team recheck its overlap hours in late March?
options: Countries such as the UK and Canada move to summer time, which changes the gap with WAT
Nigeria changes its clocks in March
Public holidays always fall in March
quiz.explain: Nigeria stays on UTC+1, but daylight saving changes in Europe and North America shift the difference.

quiz.q: A disagreement about a report deadline has gone back and forth three times in the team chat. What should the lead do?
options: Let it continue until someone gives up
Call the people involved, settle it, then post a short written outcome
Announce a new deadline without discussion
quiz.explain: After about two rounds, voice resolves tone problems faster, and the written summary keeps the team informed.

quiz.q: Which practice most builds psychological safety on a remote team?
options: Asking "Any questions?" at the end of calls
Requiring cameras on for all working hours
Thanking a member who reports a mistake early and fixing it together
Keeping problems private until they are solved
quiz.explain: Rewarding early bad news shows people they can speak up without punishment, which is the core of psychological safety.

modules.title: Tools, Workflow and Delivery
modules.overview: Here you set up the shared workspace a distributed team depends on, then follow work from a written brief to delivery with clear owners, status updates and decisions on record. The module ends with meetings that earn their time and produce a written summary everyone can rely on.

lessons.title: Designing the team workspace and a single source of truth
objectives: Map each kind of team work to one tool and one location
Design a folder structure and file naming convention others can follow
Apply basic access and security practices for shared workspaces
Choose lighter options for members with limited data or power

blocks.text: A distributed team lives inside its tools. If files sit in personal laptops, decisions are buried in private chats and tasks live in people's heads, the team spends hours searching and asking. The fix is a **single source of truth**: for each kind of information, the team agrees one place where the current, correct version lives. Everything else, including chat messages, only points to that place.

blocks.name: documents
blocks.alt: A person organising documents in folders
blocks.caption: Every kind of information needs one agreed home.

blocks.text: The five layers of a team workspace

head: Layer
Purpose
Common tools
Rule of thumb
rows: Google Drive with Docs and Sheets, Microsoft OneDrive or SharePoint
Edit the shared file; never email attachments back and forth
Trello, Asana, ClickUp, Microsoft Planner, a shared Google Sheet
If it is not on the board, it is not agreed work
Slack, Microsoft Teams, Google Chat, WhatsApp groups or Communities
Use threads; post decisions in the document, not only in chat
Google Meet, Zoom, Microsoft Teams, WhatsApp calls
A shared Google Doc, Notion, Confluence or a Google Site
Answer a repeated question once, in writing, then link to it

blocks.text: You do not need every paid tool. Many small African organisations run well on a free or low-cost Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 setup plus WhatsApp. What matters is that the team agrees which tool does which job and stops using the others for that job.

blocks.title: Layers of a team workspace
items: Messaging points to sources
Meetings produce written records
Task board shows owners
Documents hold current versions
Handbook explains how we work
blocks.caption: The written base holds the weight; chat and calls sit on top and always point down to it.

blocks.text: Folders and file names

A shared drive becomes useless when every person invents their own structure. Agree a top level by area or project, a small fixed set of subfolders, and a naming pattern. A good pattern puts the date first in **YYYY-MM-DD** form, the international ISO 8601 format, so files sort in date order on any device.

blocks.title: Worked example: tidying an NGO programme drive
blocks.context: For example, Halima runs operations for a women's livelihood programme with coordinators in Kaduna, Enugu and Oyo. The drive has files named "final report.docx", "final report 2.docx" and "FINAL final (Ngozi).docx".
steps: She creates one top-level folder per year, then one per project: "2026 / Livelihood Programme".
Inside each project she fixes five subfolders: 01 Admin, 02 Plans, 03 Field Data, 04 Reports, 05 Media.
She sets the naming pattern: date, project code, document type, version. Example: "2026-03-31_LIV_Q1-Report_v03".
She stops versions in file names for Google Docs, because Docs keep version history automatically; versions in names are kept only for PDFs sent outside.
She moves 214 old files in two afternoons and adds a one-page "How our drive works" note to the handbook.
She asks coordinators to share links, not attachments, in WhatsApp.
blocks.result: Coordinators find the current report in seconds, and nobody edits an out-of-date copy because there is only one.

blocks.text: Access and security

items: Turn on **two-step verification** for every work account, including WhatsApp, email and the drive.
Share folders with named people or the organisation, not "anyone with the link", when files contain personal data.
Give the least access needed: viewers who only read, editors who must change files.
Keep an access list. When someone leaves, remove their access the same day and transfer ownership of their files.
Store beneficiary or staff personal data only where the organisation has agreed, and collect only what is needed, in line with the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023.

blocks.title: Phishing targets shared drives
blocks.text: Fake "document shared with you" emails are a common way to steal passwords. Before signing in, check the sender address and the web address. If unsure, open the drive directly from your own bookmark, not from the email link.
Start a small handbook

The knowledge base does not need to be large on day one. Start with one shared document called "How we work" and add a page each time someone asks the same question twice. Within a few months new members can answer most of their own questions, and the leader stops being the only place where knowledge lives.

items: Our working agreement (channels, response times, overlap hours).
How our drive is organised and how to name files.
How to post a status update and where.
How to request leave or report sickness.
Who to contact for money, IT access and urgent field problems.

blocks.text: Designing for low bandwidth

Some members will work on a phone with costly data or uncertain power. Make offline access possible (Google Docs and Sheets can be made available offline on phones), keep documents text-first with compressed images, and post a short text summary with every large file so people know whether to download it. Voice notes are useful for field updates, but ask for a two-line written summary with them so the information can be searched later.

takeaways: Agree one home for each kind of information and make chat point to it.
Use a fixed folder structure and date-first (YYYY-MM-DD) file names.
Two-step verification, least access and same-day removal of leavers protect the team.
Design for phones and limited data: offline files, text summaries and light documents.

activity.title: Map and tidy your workspace
steps: List where your team currently keeps files, tasks, decisions and how-to knowledge.
Fill in the five-layer table for your team, choosing one tool per layer.
Design the folder structure and naming pattern, and rename at least ten files to fit it.
Check sharing settings on one folder that holds personal data and correct them.
activity.evidence: Your completed five-layer table, a screenshot of the renamed files and a note of the sharing changes you made.

lessons.title: From brief to delivery: owners, status updates and written decisions
objectives: Write a project brief that a remote colleague can start from without a meeting
Assign a single owner and use the DACI roles for decisions
Write a weekly async status update in a standard format
Hand over work across time zones without losing context

blocks.text: Remote work goes wrong in the gaps: unclear requests, two people each thinking the other owns a task, and decisions made on a call that half the team never hears about. A simple written workflow closes these gaps. It has four parts: a **brief** at the start, a single **owner** for each piece of work, a regular **status update**, and a **decision record** when choices are made.

blocks.name: task-list
blocks.alt: A person checking items on a task list
blocks.caption: Clear owners and written status keep remote work moving.

blocks.title: Remote delivery workflow
items: Written brief
Owner and deadline
Weekly status update
Decisions logged
Delivery and review
blocks.caption: Every stage leaves a written trace that someone in another time zone can pick up.

blocks.text: The one-page brief

items: **Goal:** what success looks like, in one or two sentences.
**Deliverable:** exactly what will be handed over, in what format.
**Audience or user:** who it is for.
**Deadline and milestones**, with time zone.
**Constraints:** budget, brand rules, data rules, tools.
**Owner and reviewers:** who does it, who checks it, who approves.
**Links:** previous examples, data, templates.

blocks.text: One owner, clear decision roles

Every task needs one named owner, sometimes called the **DRI** (directly responsible individual). Others can help, but one person is accountable for moving it forward. For decisions, the **DACI** framework from Atlassian's Team Playbook gives four roles: the **Driver** gathers information and gets the decision made by the agreed date; the **Approver** is the one person who decides; **Contributors** give expert input, a voice but not a vote; and the **Informed** are told once it is decided. Naming these roles in writing ends the common remote problem of decisions that are discussed for weeks and never made.
The weekly async status update
Replace most status meetings with a written update posted on a fixed day, in the same format every time, so readers know where to look. A widely used structure is:

items: **Status line:** On track, At risk or Off track, with one sentence why.
**Done this week:** finished items with links.
**Next week:** planned items with owners and dates.
**Blocked or at risk:** what is stuck, who can unblock it, by when.
**Decisions needed:** the question, options, recommendation and Approver.

blocks.title: Worked example: a status update and a DACI decision
blocks.context: For example, Kemi owns a community health awareness campaign run by a team in Lagos, Port Harcourt and Accra. It is Friday and she posts her update in the campaign channel and the project document.
steps: Status: At risk. Radio slots are booked but the flyer artwork is 3 days late.
Done: 4 of 6 radio jingles recorded (links); volunteer list confirmed at 38 people.
Next: Seun in Port Harcourt records the last 2 jingles by Wednesday; Kwame in Accra finalises the flyer by Tuesday 5 pm WAT (4 pm in Accra, which is UTC+0).

Blocked: printing takes 5 working days; if Kwame delivers on Tuesday, flyers are ready the following Tuesday (Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Monday, Tuesday), which is distribution day itself, with no buffer.

Decision needed, using DACI: print 5,000 flyers at about 45 naira each (about 225,000 naira) or 3,000 at about 55 naira each (about 165,000 naira); quotes approximate. Driver: Kemi. Approver: the programme manager, Bola. Contributors: finance and Seun. Informed: all volunteers.
Kemi recommends 3,000 flyers, because 38 volunteers can realistically hand out about 80 each, which is 3,040 flyers.
blocks.result: Bola approves the 3,000 option in a comment on Saturday. Kemi logs the decision with date, Approver and reason, and the volunteers are told on Monday.

blocks.text: Handovers across time zones

When work passes from one person to another at the end of their day, sometimes called a follow-the-sun handover, the receiver must be able to continue without asking anything. A good handover note says what was done, the exact state now, what to do next, known risks and where the files are. Write it in the task or document, not only in chat.

blocks.title: Red early is better than green late
blocks.text: Mark work At risk the moment you doubt the date. Leaders can usually fix a problem with three days' notice; they rarely can with three hours.
A handover note that works

items: **Done:** "Cleaned the March attendance sheet; 214 rows, duplicates removed."
**State now:** "Draft chart is in the Q1 Report document, section 3, not yet checked."
**Next action:** "Check the Oyo totals against the field forms in 03 Field Data, then share with Bola."
**Risks:** "Two Oyo forms were unreadable photos; I asked the coordinator to resend."
**Where:** links to every file mentioned.

blocks.text: Common brief mistakes are just as predictable: no deadline time zone, two people named as owner, no link to previous examples, and a goal written as an activity ("run a campaign") instead of a result ("3,000 flyers reach women in four markets by 30 April"). Read your brief once as if you were new to the team, and fix anything you would need to ask about.

takeaways: Start work from a one-page written brief.
Give every task one owner and every decision a Driver and a single Approver (DACI).
Post a weekly status update in a fixed format: status, done, next, blocked, decisions needed.
Handover notes must let the next person continue without asking.

activity.title: Brief, update and decide
steps: Write a one-page brief for a real or practice piece of work using the seven brief headings.
Write one weekly status update for it in the five-part format.
Include one decision in DACI form, naming each role and your recommendation.
Ask a colleague to read both without explanation and note any question they still have.
activity.evidence: The brief, the status update with its DACI decision, and the colleague's questions with how you fixed the gaps.

lessons.title: Meetings that earn their time: agendas, roles and written summaries
objectives: Decide whether a topic needs a meeting at all
Write an agenda that states the outcome needed for each item
Run a remote meeting with clear roles and inclusive habits
Produce a written summary and decision log entry within one working day

blocks.text: Remote meetings are expensive. A one-hour call with eight people uses eight hours of the team's time, plus the focus lost before and after, plus data costs for people on mobile connections. In an async-first team a meeting has to earn its place. Before you book one, ask: could this be a document with comments? If the honest answer is yes, write the document.

blocks.name: remote-meeting
blocks.alt: People joining a video meeting from different screens
blocks.caption: A good remote meeting starts before the call and ends with a written record.

blocks.text: When a meeting is the right tool

blocks.title: Meet or write?
items: Meet live
Write async
blocks.caption: If a topic sits on the right, a document with comments is usually faster and fairer.

blocks.text: An agenda that drives outcomes

Post the agenda at least 24 hours before, in the shared meeting document, with pre-reads linked. Write each item as a question with the outcome you need: decide, agree, gather input or inform. Put a time against each item and the name of the person leading it. If there is no agenda, it is reasonable for people to ask for one or to decline.

head: Time
Item
Outcome needed
Lead
rows: Check-in: one word on how you are
Which two states pilot the new reporting form? (pre-read: options doc)

blocks.text: Roles in the call

items: **Facilitator:** keeps to the agenda, invites quieter people by name, parks off-topic issues.
**Note-taker:** writes decisions and actions live in the shared document so everyone can see them.
**Timekeeper:** warns at the halfway and two-minute points of each item.
**Decision owner:** for each decision item, the Approver who confirms the choice aloud.

blocks.text: Rotate these roles so the same person, often the most junior woman in the room, is not always the note-taker. Start on time, and do not repeat the meeting for late joiners; the live notes will catch them up. If you record the call, tell everyone at the start and explain where the recording will be kept and for how long, because recordings contain personal data.
The written summary

The meeting is not finished until the summary is posted, ideally the same day and certainly within one working day. People who could not attend should be able to act on it. Keep it short: decisions, actions with owners and dates, open questions, and a link to the full notes. Then copy each decision into the team's **decision log**, a simple table with date, decision, Approver, reason and link.

blocks.title: Worked example: costing and summarising a weekly call
blocks.context: For example, Ruth leads a seven-person regional team that met for 60 minutes every Monday. She wants to know what the meeting costs and whether it can be shorter.
steps: Time cost: 7 people x 1 hour = 7 person-hours a week; over 4 weeks that is 28 person-hours.
She moves status updates to a written Friday post, which removes 25 minutes of reading out updates.
The new call is 30 minutes for decisions and risks only: 7 x 0.5 = 3.5 person-hours a week, 14 a month, saving 14 person-hours a month.

After the next call she posts: Decisions: Kaduna and Ekiti pilot the new form (Approver: Ruth). Actions: Ada sends the form to both coordinators by Wednesday; Musa lists June training risks in the risk sheet by Thursday. Open: venue for Ekiti, Musa to propose by next Monday.
She adds the pilot decision to the decision log with the reason: both states already use smartphones for reporting.
blocks.result: The team halves its meeting time, and people who missed the call act on the summary the same afternoon.

blocks.title: The two-minute read-back
blocks.text: End every meeting by having the note-taker read the actions aloud with owners and dates. It catches misunderstandings while everyone is still on the call.
Inclusive and hybrid calls

items: Share the agenda and pre-reads early so people with slower connections can download them in advance.
Allow cameras off when data or power is limited; ask for audio and chat contributions instead.
Use the chat or a shared document for round-robin input, so quieter people can write rather than interrupt.
In hybrid meetings, give remote people the first turn on each item, and have one person in the room watch the chat.
Keep calls under an hour; for longer work sessions, schedule a 10-minute break.

blocks.text: Hybrid meetings, where some people sit together in a room and others join online, are the hardest to run fairly. The people in the room talk to each other, side conversations are lost, and remote members struggle to break in. A simple rule many remote teams use is "one person, one screen": if anyone is remote, everyone joins from their own device, even people in the same office, so all voices sound and look equal. When that is not possible, use one good room microphone and a facilitator who reads the chat aloud.

takeaways: Count meeting cost in person-hours, and turn status meetings into written updates.
Agenda items are questions with a stated outcome, posted 24 hours ahead with pre-reads.
Use and rotate roles: facilitator, note-taker, timekeeper, decision owner.
Post a summary within one working day and log every decision.

activity.title: Run one meeting properly
steps: Choose a real or practice meeting and decide in writing why it needs to be live.
Post an agenda 24 hours ahead using the four-column format.
Run the meeting with named roles and a read-back of actions.
Post the summary within one working day and add the decisions to a decision log.
activity.evidence: The agenda, the posted summary with a time stamp, and your decision log with at least one entry.

quiz.q: A coordinator keeps editing a downloaded copy of the budget and emailing it back. What is the best fix?
options: Ask her to rename the file "final"
Make the shared Sheet the single source of truth and share a link instead of attachments
quiz.explain: One shared, current file removes conflicting copies; chat and email should only point to it.

quiz.q: Which file name follows the convention taught in this module?
quiz.explain: Date first in YYYY-MM-DD form, then project, type and version, so files sort correctly everywhere.

quiz.q: In DACI, who makes the final decision?
quiz.explain: There is one Approver. The Driver gathers input and gets the decision made by the agreed date.

quiz.q: Kemi suspects on Monday that a Friday deadline will slip. According to the module, what should she do?
options: Wait until Friday in case it works out
Mark the work At risk now and say what would unblock it
Quietly work at night to catch up
Remove the task from the board
quiz.explain: Flagging early gives leaders time to help. Red early is better than green late.

quiz.q: A 45-minute weekly call has 8 people. How many person-hours does it use in 4 weeks?
quiz.explain: 8 people x 0.75 hours = 6 person-hours a week; 6 x 4 weeks = 24 person-hours.

quiz.q: Which item is best handled by a meeting rather than a document?
options: Feedback to a colleague whose work upset a partner
quiz.explain: Sensitive feedback needs tone and dialogue, which a live conversation handles better than text.

modules.title: Diagnosing, Improving and Leading Distributed Teams
modules.overview: In this final module you learn to assess how well a distributed team is working, scope and price an improvement plan as a consultant or internal lead, and build the personal accountability system and evidence portfolio that show you can be trusted with remote leadership.

lessons.title: Diagnosing a distributed team: discovery questions and a collaboration audit
objectives: Ask discovery questions that reveal how a remote team really works
Score a team on eight collaboration areas using evidence
Prioritise fixes using an impact and effort matrix
Write a short findings summary for a team leader

blocks.text: Whether you are joining a new remote team, taking over as its lead, or being invited to advise an organisation, your first job is to understand how work actually flows today. Teams often describe the way they wish they worked. Your job is to find the way they really work, using questions and evidence, before you suggest anything.

blocks.name: interview
blocks.alt: Two people in a discovery conversation
blocks.caption: Good diagnosis starts with listening and asking for evidence.

blocks.text: Discovery questions

head: Area
Question to ask
Evidence to request
rows: When you need a quick answer, where do you ask, and how long do you usually wait?
A week of messages in the main group (with permission)
Where is the current version of the budget or workplan? Show me.
Time taken to find it during the conversation
For this project, who owns each piece?
The task board, or a list if none exists
How do you know what colleagues in other locations did this week?
Which regular meetings exist, how long are they, what comes out of them?
What was the last important decision, who made it, and where is it recorded?
What did your newest member receive in their first week?
When do people send messages? Who rarely speaks in calls?
Message time stamps; one call observation

blocks.text: Talk to people at different levels and locations, not only the leader, and speak to at least one person who joined recently. New joiners notice gaps that long-serving staff no longer see. Keep what people tell you confidential and report patterns, not names.
Scoring the audit

Score each of the eight areas from 1 to 5 using the evidence: 1 means no shared practice, 3 means a practice exists but is used unevenly, 5 means a written practice that most people follow. Scores are a tool for conversation, not a verdict, so show the evidence behind each number.

blocks.title: Worked example: auditing a volunteer network
blocks.context: For example, Grace is asked to review a women's volunteer network with coordinators in six Nigerian states and two in Ghana. She interviews nine people and reviews two weeks of messages and documents.
steps: Scores: Channels 2, Source of truth 1, Ownership 3, Updates 2, Meetings 3, Decisions 1, Onboarding 2, Wellbeing and inclusion 3.
Total is 2 + 1 + 3 + 2 + 3 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 17 out of a possible 40; the average is 17 / 8 = 2.1.
Evidence for Source of truth: it took 11 minutes and three people to find the current volunteer list, and two versions disagreed by 23 names.
Evidence for Decisions: a change to the reporting date was agreed on a call but never written down; three coordinators missed it.
Evidence for Wellbeing: 40% of the group messages she reviewed (62 of 155) were sent after 9 pm, often by the same two coordinators.
blocks.result: Grace reports that the two lowest areas, Source of truth and Decisions, are causing visible errors, and recommends starting there.

blocks.text: Choosing what to fix first

Do not try to fix everything. Place each possible improvement on an **impact and effort matrix**: how much it would help, against how hard it is to do. Start with high-impact, low-effort quick wins, plan the high-impact, high-effort projects, and drop most low-impact work.

blocks.title: Impact and effort matrix
items: Quick wins: do now
Big projects: plan carefully
Small tidy-ups: if time
Avoid: low value, costly
blocks.caption: A decision log is a quick win; moving the whole organisation to a new tool is a big project.

blocks.text: For Grace's network, a shared decision log and one master volunteer list are quick wins: a few hours each, with immediate effect. A full handbook is a big project for the following quarter. Buying a paid project tool is in the avoid box for now, because the problem is habit, not software.
The findings summary

items: One-sentence overall picture, for example "Strong commitment, weak shared records."
The scores table with one line of evidence per area.
Top three recommendations, each with owner, effort and expected effect.
What you did not look at, so the leader knows the limits of the review.
A proposed date to re-score in 60 to 90 days.

blocks.title: Handle message reviews carefully
blocks.text: Reading a team's chats can expose personal information. Get written permission from the organisation, tell members a review is happening, look only at work channels, and never copy private details into your report.
When you are the new member

The same questions help when you join a remote team rather than advise one. In your first week ask your manager or a buddy: Which channel do I use for what? How quickly do people expect replies? Where are decisions recorded? Which meetings must I attend and which are optional? What does a good weekly update look like here? Write the answers down. If no working agreement exists, your notes can become the first draft of one, which is a useful early contribution.

takeaways: Ask for evidence, not just opinions: "show me where the current version is".
Interview across levels and locations, including a recent joiner.
Score eight areas from 1 to 5 and show the evidence for each score.
Start with high-impact, low-effort fixes and state the limits of your review.

activity.title: Run a mini audit
steps: Choose a team you belong to or a practice case.
Ask at least four of the discovery questions to two or more people.
Score all eight areas from 1 to 5 with one line of evidence each, and compute the total and average.
Place at least five possible fixes on an impact and effort matrix.
Write a one-page findings summary using the five-step outline.
activity.evidence: Your scores table with evidence, the matrix and the one-page summary.

lessons.title: Scoping, pricing and protecting a collaboration improvement project
objectives: Turn audit findings into a scoped improvement project with deliverables
Estimate effort in days and calculate a fair project price
Write a short proposal with acceptance criteria and payment terms
Handle extra requests with a written change request

blocks.text: After an audit, the leader usually asks: "Can you help us fix this?" You might answer as an external consultant who charges a fee, or as an internal lead who must win time and support from management. Either way, the same discipline applies: define exactly what will be delivered, estimate the effort honestly, agree how success will be judged, and protect the scope from quietly growing.

blocks.name: signed-document
blocks.caption: A short written scope protects both you and the client.

blocks.text: From findings to deliverables

Turn each recommendation into something that can be handed over and checked. "Improve communication" is not a deliverable. "A one-page working agreement, agreed by all coordinators and published in the handbook" is. Good deliverables for this kind of project include a working agreement, a tidied shared drive with naming rules, a decision log template, a status update template, a meeting format, a short handbook, and training sessions with recordings or notes.

blocks.title: From audit to agreed project
items: Audit findings
Deliverables and acceptance criteria
Effort estimate in days
Price and payment terms
Signed scope
blocks.caption: Every price should trace back to named deliverables and estimated days.

blocks.text: Estimating and pricing

A simple, defensible method is a **day rate** multiplied by estimated days. Work out your day rate from the income you need and the days you can realistically bill. Remember that as an independent consultant you will not bill every working day: some days go to finding clients, admin, learning and rest. Add a small contingency for unknowns, and say clearly what is not included.

blocks.title: Worked example: pricing a 10-day engagement
blocks.context: For example, Bimpe is an independent remote-operations consultant in Ibadan. An Abuja-based NGO with 15 staff across four states asks her to fix the problems found in her audit. The figures below are illustrative, not market rates.
steps: Day rate: she aims for 800,000 naira a month before costs and expects to bill about 10 days a month, so 800,000 / 10 = 80,000 naira per day.

Effort: audit already done; working agreement workshop and drafting 2 days; drive restructure and naming rules 3 days; templates for status updates, meetings and decision log 2 days; two 2-hour training sessions with preparation 2 days; 30-day follow-up review 1 day. Total: 2 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 10 days.
Base price: 10 x 80,000 = 800,000 naira.
Contingency of 10% for unknowns: 800,000 x 0.10 = 80,000 naira, giving a fixed price of 880,000 naira.
Payment terms: 50% on signing (440,000 naira) and 50% on acceptance of the deliverables (440,000 naira), paid by bank transfer to her business account.
Out of scope, written in the proposal: buying or configuring paid software, migrating email systems, and work for teams outside the four states.
blocks.result: The NGO accepts a clear, traceable price. Both sides know exactly what 880,000 naira buys.

blocks.text: Acceptance criteria

For each deliverable, agree how it will be judged finished. For example: "Working agreement: signed off by the programme manager and posted in the handbook"; "Drive: all current-year files moved into the new structure and three coordinators can find the current budget in under one minute". Acceptance criteria stop the endless "just one more change" at the end of a project.
Protecting the scope

Scope creep is when extra work slips in without extra time or money. In remote projects it often arrives as a casual WhatsApp message: "While you are at it, can you also set up the board for the finance team?" Do not refuse and do not silently agree. Reply that you are happy to help and will send a short change request.

items: Describe the new request in one or two sentences.
Estimate extra days and cost: for example, 2 extra days x 80,000 = 160,000 naira.
State the effect on the timeline, for example the final review moves by one week.
Ask the approver named in the contract to accept in writing (an email reply is enough).
Start the extra work only after written approval, and log it with the project decisions.

blocks.title: Payments and fraud
blocks.text: Confirm bank details by phone with a known contact before any transfer, and be suspicious of sudden "new account" instructions by email or WhatsApp, a common fraud pattern. If you are registered with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) as a business name or company, invoice in that name so payments go to your business account.

blocks.title: If you are an internal lead
blocks.text: Use the same structure in an internal proposal, replacing the price with the hours you and others will need, and the payment terms with the approval you need from management.
The one-page proposal

Keep the proposal short enough to read on a phone: the problem in two sentences using audit evidence; the deliverables with acceptance criteria; the timeline by week; the price, contingency and payment terms; what is out of scope; how changes will be handled; and the names of the client Approver and your own contact details. Send it as a PDF and ask for written acceptance by email, which becomes your record.

takeaways: Turn findings into named deliverables, each with acceptance criteria.
Price = day rate x estimated days, plus a stated contingency; list what is out of scope.
Agree payment terms such as 50% on signing and 50% on acceptance.
Handle extra requests with a written change request before starting the work.

activity.title: Write a one-page proposal
steps: Take the top three recommendations from your mini audit.
Turn each into a deliverable with an acceptance criterion.
Estimate days for each, calculate a price from a day rate you can justify (or hours for an internal proposal), and add contingency.
List at least three items that are out of scope.
Draft a sample change request for one likely extra request.
activity.evidence: The one-page proposal showing your arithmetic and the sample change request.

lessons.title: Your accountability system, leadership portfolio and 90-day plan
objectives: Set up a personal system to capture, plan and review your commitments
Use start-of-day and end-of-day posts to keep your work visible
Measure your own reliability with a simple commitment tracker
Assemble a three-piece evidence portfolio and a 90-day plan

blocks.text: Leaders of distributed teams are trusted when their own work is reliable and visible. Nobody walks past your desk to see that you are busy, so you need a personal system that keeps track of every promise and makes progress easy for others to see. This lesson helps you build that system and then package your evidence for employers, clients or your own organisation.

blocks.name: deep-work
blocks.alt: A person concentrating on focused work at a desk
blocks.caption: A personal system frees your mind for focused work.

blocks.text: Capture, plan, do, review

David Allen's Getting Things Done (GTD) method is a widely used personal productivity approach. Its core idea is that your mind is for having ideas, not holding them: capture every commitment into one trusted list, decide the next action, organise it, and review the system weekly. You can run it in a notebook, Google Tasks, Microsoft To Do or a simple sheet.

blocks.title: Weekly accountability cycle
items: Capture every commitment
Plan the week Monday
Time-block focus work
Post visible updates
Review on Friday
blocks.caption: The Friday review feeds the next Monday plan, so nothing promised is forgotten.

items: **Capture:** every time you say "I will" in a message or call, add it to your list within the hour, with a date.
**Plan Monday:** choose the three most important outcomes for the week and block time for them in your calendar, inside your best working hours.
**Protect focus:** set your status to Focus during those blocks and mute non-urgent channels, as your working agreement allows.

**Make it visible:** post a short start-of-day line ("Today: finish the Q1 report draft, review Musa's budget") and an end-of-day line ("Done: draft shared. Tomorrow: budget review. Blocked: none") in the team channel if your team uses them.
**Review Friday:** check every commitment, close finished ones, renegotiate any that will slip before their date, and write next week's top three.

blocks.text: Measure your reliability

Keep a simple commitment tracker: date promised, what, due date, outcome (on time, renegotiated early, late). Review it monthly. The goal is not perfection but honesty: a commitment changed early with a reason is far better for trust than one missed silently.

blocks.title: Worked example: four weeks of commitments
blocks.context: For example, Uche coordinates a remote training team and tracks every commitment she makes for four weeks.
steps: She records 14 commitments in total.
12 were delivered on time, 1 was renegotiated two days before its due date, and 1 was delivered late without warning.
On-time rate: 12 / 14 = 0.857, about 86%.
Kept or renegotiated early: 13 / 14 = 0.929, about 93%.
She looks at the late item: it was promised in a voice call and never captured in her list.
Her fix: after every call she spends two minutes moving any "I will" into her list before doing anything else.
blocks.result: The next month Uche records 15 commitments with none late without warning, and her team lead notices she is easy to rely on.

blocks.text: Your evidence portfolio

Remote employers and clients increasingly ask for proof of how you work, not just a CV. Build a short portfolio, as a shared folder or a page on a free site such as Google Sites, containing three pieces. Remove names and personal or confidential details from real documents, or use practice versions.

head: Piece
What it shows
Include
rows: You write clearly for readers in other places and times
One weekly update with status, done, next, blocked, decisions needed
You run meetings that produce decisions
Agenda, posted summary and decision log entry for the same meeting
You keep promises and make work visible
Screenshot of your list, one weekly review note, your commitment tracker summary

blocks.text: Add a half-page reflection: what you changed, what improved and what you would do differently. Concrete, honest reflection is more convincing than claims like "excellent communicator".
Boundaries protect reliability

Remote work can quietly stretch into every evening, especially when colleagues are in other time zones. A reliable leader is a rested one. Set clear end-of-day times in your calendar and status, turn off notifications for non-urgent channels outside working hours, and use scheduled sending so your late-night messages arrive in the morning. If you lead others, model this yourself: when the leader replies at midnight, the team believes midnight replies are expected.
Your 90-day plan

items: **Days 1 to 30:** run your accountability cycle every week; publish or update a working agreement with one team.
**Days 31 to 60:** run a mini audit on a team you belong to and deliver two quick wins, such as a decision log and a status update template.

**Days 61 to 90:** re-score the team, write a one-page before-and-after case study, and add it to your portfolio; apply for at least one remote coordination or team lead role, or offer the improvement project to one organisation.

takeaways: Capture every "I will" into one trusted list within the hour.
Plan on Monday, time-block focus work, review on Friday.
Start-of-day and end-of-day posts make remote work visible.
Track commitments monthly; renegotiate early instead of missing silently.
A three-piece portfolio with honest reflection proves your remote skills.

activity.title: Build and test your system for two weeks
steps: Choose one list tool and one calendar and set up your commitment tracker.
Run the Monday plan and Friday review for two weeks, posting start and end-of-day lines on at least five days.
Calculate your on-time rate and your kept-or-renegotiated-early rate.
Write your 90-day plan with dates for each 30-day stage.
activity.evidence: Your tracker with both percentages, two Friday review notes and your dated 90-day plan.

quiz.q: During an audit, a leader says "Our files are well organised." What should you do next?
options: Write it down as a strength
Ask a different leader the same question
Ask them to show you where the current workplan is and note how long it takes
quiz.explain: Audits rely on evidence. Watching someone find the current version tests the claim directly.

quiz.q: A team scores 3, 2, 4, 1, 3, 2, 2, 3 across the eight audit areas. What is the average?
quiz.explain: The total is 20; 20 divided by 8 areas is 2.5.

quiz.q: Which improvement is usually a quick win on the impact and effort matrix?
options: Moving the whole organisation to a new paid tool
quiz.explain: A decision log takes a few hours and immediately stops decisions being lost.

quiz.q: A consultant's day rate is 70,000 naira. She estimates 8 days plus 10% contingency. What is the fixed price?
Midway through a project the client sends a WhatsApp asking you to also train two extra teams. What is the best response?
options: Do it quietly to keep the client happy
Stop work until the contract ends
Welcome the request and send a written change request with extra days, cost and timeline effect
quiz.explain: A change request protects the scope and the relationship: the client decides with full information.

quiz.q: Uche made 20 commitments in a month: 17 on time, 2 renegotiated early and 1 late without warning. What is her kept-or-renegotiated-early rate?

finalQuiz.q: Which situation most clearly calls for a synchronous conversation?
options: A team member is hurt by a public comment on her work
finalQuiz.explain: Emotion and possible conflict are handled best live, where tone is clear; the outcome can then be written down.

finalQuiz.q: An Abuja team works 9 am to 5 pm WAT and a Toronto partner works 9 am to 5 pm local time. In January (Toronto UTC-5), when do their hours overlap in Lagos time?
finalQuiz.explain: Toronto 9 am is 14:00 UTC, which is 3 pm WAT. Abuja finishes at 5 pm WAT, so the overlap is 3 pm to 5 pm.

finalQuiz.q: What belongs in a team working agreement?
options: Channels, response times, overlap hours, where files live and a review date
finalQuiz.explain: The agreement makes communication expectations explicit and is reviewed regularly.

finalQuiz.q: Why should leaders avoid judging remote staff by hours shown online?
options: Trust rests on delivered commitments and early flags, and surveillance tends to damage trust
Hours do not matter at all in any job
finalQuiz.explain: Outcomes, visible work and honest renegotiation build trust; presence monitoring usually undermines it.

finalQuiz.q: A coordinator posts a 20 MB video for colleagues on limited data. What should she add?
options: A request to watch it immediately
A short text summary so people can decide whether to download it
A second copy of the video
finalQuiz.explain: A text summary respects data costs and keeps the key information searchable.

finalQuiz.q: When a staff member leaves, what should happen to their access to the shared drive?
options: Leave it in case they return
Remove it the same day and transfer ownership of their files
finalQuiz.explain: Same-day removal and ownership transfer protect team data and keep files available.

finalQuiz.q: In a weekly status update, where should a request for approval go?
options: Under Decisions needed, with options, a recommendation and the Approver named
Hidden at the end of the Done section
In a separate private chat only
It should not be in the update
finalQuiz.explain: A dedicated Decisions needed section makes the ask visible and assigns it to the right person.

finalQuiz.q: In DACI, what role do Contributors have?
options: They give expert input but do not decide
finalQuiz.explain: Contributors have a voice but not a vote; the single Approver decides.

finalQuiz.q: A meeting ended an hour ago. What should the team find in the shared space by the next working day?
options: A written summary of decisions, actions with owners and dates, open questions, and decision log entries
finalQuiz.explain: The written summary lets everyone, including absent members, act on the meeting.

finalQuiz.q: In an audit, a team scores 1 on Decisions and 4 on Meetings. Where should improvement probably start?
options: Meetings, because it is already good
Decisions, especially with a quick win like a decision log
finalQuiz.explain: The lowest-scoring area with a high-impact, low-effort fix is the sensible starting point.

finalQuiz.q: A consultant charges 75,000 naira a day for 12 days with 50% paid on signing. How much is paid on signing?
finalQuiz.explain: 12 x 75,000 = 900,000 naira; 50% of that is 450,000 naira.

finalQuiz.q: You realise on Tuesday you cannot deliver a report due Thursday. What does a strong accountability habit require?
options: Say nothing and hope for an extension
Tell the owner now, give a new date and a reason, and record it in your tracker
Deliver a rushed version without telling anyone
Wait for your manager to ask
finalQuiz.explain: Renegotiating early keeps trust; missing silently damages it.

capstone.title: Remote Collaboration Practice Portfolio
capstone.brief: Produce a portfolio that proves you can work and lead in a distributed team: a complete asynchronous status update, a meeting pack (agenda, written summary and decision log entry), and a personal accountability system tested for at least two weeks, plus a working agreement, a short team audit and a reflection with your 90-day plan.
steps: Choose a real team, volunteer group or practice project with at least three people in more than one location.
Draft and agree a one-page working agreement including overlap hours calculated in UTC.
Write one weekly asynchronous status update in the five-part format, including one DACI decision.
Plan and run one meeting: post the agenda 24 hours ahead, use named roles, post the summary within one working day and log decisions.
Run your personal accountability cycle for two weeks and calculate your on-time and kept-or-renegotiated-early rates.
Score the team on the eight audit areas and propose your top three improvements.
Remove personal and confidential details, assemble everything in one shared folder or page, and write a half-page reflection and a 90-day plan.
evidence: Async status update with status line, done, next, blocked and decisions needed
Meeting agenda with outcomes per item, posted summary with time stamp, and decision log entry
Accountability system screenshots, two Friday review notes and commitment tracker with both percentages
Working agreement with UTC overlap calculation
Audit scores table with evidence and three prioritised recommendations
